evidence.label: The Isoperimetric Conjecture for the Cubic Flat Three-Torus

headline: Proves the isoperimetric conjecture for the cubic flat three-torus: balls, tubes, slabs and their complements.
scope: Finite-perimeter regions of every volume in the unit cubic flat three-torus ℝ³/ℤ³, including the equality cases at the two transition volumes.
plain: Picture a cube whose opposite faces are glued, so leaving one face brings you back through the opposite one. The question is how to enclose a given volume inside it with the least surface area. The paper proves the long-standing guess: small volumes use a ball, middle volumes a tube around a straight loop, and larger ones a flat slab. Past half the volume, the answers are the complements of these. A Lean proof covers the full result.
doesNot: This does not treat flat tori of other shapes, such as non-cubic boxes, or higher dimensions.
origin: This result comes from an unreleased OpenAI model, published in the openai/math release on 6 October 2026.

scorecard.firstStepBy: Hauswirth, Pérez, Romon and Ros, who state the ball–tube–slab prediction explicitly
scorecard.significanceWhy: It settles a concrete, well-known periodic isoperimetric problem and classifies every minimizer, including the transition cases.

explanation:
Start with a unit cube whose opposite faces are glued. A bug leaving through the top comes back through the bottom. This space is the cubic flat three-torus. Now enclose one tenth of its volume with as little surface area as you can. A ball has surface area (36π)^(1/3) × 0.1^(2/3), about 1.042. A solid tube around a straight loop that closes up through two faces has area 2√(0.1π), about 1.121. A slab between two parallel faces always has area 2. At volume 0.1 the ball wins.

At volume one quarter, the ball needs about 1.919 and the tube about 1.772. The tube now wins. At larger volumes the slab wins, since its area stays at 2. The guess was that the best shape always follows this order. It appears in work of Hauswirth, Pérez, Romon and Ros[1]. Some pieces were known. Balls win for small enough volumes, by Morgan and Johnson[2]. Slabs are the only winners near half the volume, by Acerbi, Fusco and Morini[3]. But those results did not reach the switching volumes[4]. Milman reduced the full guess to checking just two volumes[5].

The paper proves the full guess[6]. The least area at volume V is the smallest of the three numbers above[6]. Above one half, use 1 − V in place of V. The ball wins up to volume 4π/81, about 0.155. There the ball has radius 1/3, the tube radius 2/9, and both have area 4π/9, about 1.396. The tube wins up to volume 1/π, about 0.318. There tube and slab both have area 2. Then the slab wins up to one half. Past one half, the winners are the complements[7]. At each switch both shapes win and nothing else does[8].

The remaining difficulty was to rule out a surface with handles, of higher genus, that might do better[9]. The new ingredient slices a possible rival by parallel planes near the tube–slab switch[10]. Nesting of those slices forces extra length in some of them, which adds up to too much area. Explicit arithmetic bounds finish the last one-variable estimate[11].

How sure is this? The Lean scope note says the formalization determines the least-area profile and all minimizers in the unit cubic flat three-torus. It includes every equality case at the volumes 4π/81 and 1/π. No specialist review has been published.
hypeCheck: Solid. Lean covers the full profile and the classification of minimizers, including the transition cases. No specialist review is published.

glossary.meaning: A cube with opposite faces glued, so that moving out through one face brings you back through the opposite one.
The question of how to enclose a fixed volume with the least boundary area.
The least boundary area needed to enclose each volume.
A region that achieves the least boundary area for its volume.
A shortest straight loop in the torus, here a line that runs across the cube parallel to one edge.
The region between two parallel flat faces of the cube.
The number of handles of a surface; a sphere has genus 0 and a doughnut surface genus 1.

claims.sourceQuote: For \(0<V\le1/2\), every minimizing region is, up to an ambient isometry and a null set, one of the following: \[ \begin{array}{c|c} \text{volume range}&\text{region}\\ \hline 0<V\le 4\pi/81 & \text{a ball of radius }(3V/(4\pi))^{1/3}\\[2pt] 4\pi/81\le V\le1/\pi &\text{a solid circular tube of radius }\sqrt{V/\pi}\\ &\text{about a shortest closed geodesic}\\[2pt] 1/\pi\le V\le1/2 &\text{a slab of width }V\text{ between coordinate tori}. \end{array} \] Both listed types occur at each common endpoint of adjacent ranges, and there are no further equality cases.
